title: The Potala
hookLine: the great palace on the hill in Lhasa

cards: Walls, white and then deep red, rising out of the rock as if the hill grew them. Windows in long rows, stairs zigzagging up the face, gold roofs at the very top catching the thin, bright air. Below it, the city of Lhasa.
Pilgrims walk around the hill's foot, turning prayer wheels, and look up. For a long time this was the home of the Dalai Lamas, and the place from which Tibet was governed.

teach.b: Start with the name. Tradition says Potala comes from Potalaka, the mountain where, in Buddhist texts, Avalokiteshvara dwells.
Tibetans regard the Dalai Lamas as an emanation of Chenrezig, Avalokiteshvara, so the palace was named for his mountain: the bodhisattva's mountain, brought to Lhasa.

teach.h: THE GREAT FIFTH BUILDS ON OLD GROUND.
teach.b: The Great Fifth began it as his seat. Tradition says a palace of Tibet's early king Songtsen Gampo once stood on the same hill, so the new building rose on old ground. Then the two colors.
The White Palace held the offices and living rooms, where government and daily life went on.
The Red Palace, rising in the middle, is given over to religion: chapels, halls, and the golden tombs of past Dalai Lamas, built as stupas.

teach.h: WHITE FOR WORK, RED FOR PRAYER.
teach.b: The two roles we met yesterday, side by side: worldly work in white, the spiritual heart in red.

teach.h: WHERE THE CITY CAN SEE IT.
teach.b: And a palace on a hill stands where the city can see it. Someone carrying water, someone haggling at a market stall, someone walking home at dusk, can turn and see it.
A building like that becomes a reminder, whether you ask for one or not.
Some pilgrims walk the circuit around the hill, keeping it on their right, the way Buddhists walk around a stupa. They don't have to go in. Circling it is the practice.

how: Pilgrims in Lhasa walk the circuit around the Potala's hill clockwise, often spinning prayer wheels and reciting mantras, and visit its chapels and the tombs of past Dalai Lamas.

games.q: you're a pilgrim at the foot of the Potala's hill. the doors are far above. what do you do?
o: walk around the hill, keeping it on your right.
turn back, since you can't go in.
games.why: walking the circuit is a practice in itself, the same way Buddhists walk around a stupa.

practice: Imagine you're standing in a street in Lhasa, busy with your own errand, and you lift your eyes: white walls, then red, the gold at the top. Stay with that view for a few breaths, then look back down to the street.
Whenever your mind wanders, lift your eyes again, and let the hill be there.

wordCard.voice: The Potala. The palace on the hill in Lhasa, named for Avalokiteshvara's mountain, white for the work of governing and red for prayer.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Potalaka, the mountain where Avalokiteshvara dwells; the palace takes its name.
